```{=html}
<style>
  .term { border-bottom: 1px dotted currentColor; cursor: help; }
</style>
<script>
const GLOSSARY = {
  pca: "Principal Component Analysis: boils many benchmark scores down to a few summary numbers while keeping as much of the difference between models as possible.",
  pc: "Principal component: one of those summary numbers. PC1 captures the biggest differences between models, PC2 the next biggest, and so on.",
  variance: "Explained variance: the share of all the differences between models that this axis captures. Higher means the axis tells more of the story.",
  standardized: "Standardized: each benchmark is rescaled to the same range so they can be compared, even if one is scored out of 100 and another out of 1.",
  loading: "Loading: how strongly a benchmark pushes models along a principal component. Big positive or negative values mean that benchmark matters a lot for that axis.",
  umap: "UMAP: places models with similar score patterns near each other. Good at showing clusters, but the axes and the distances between far-apart clusters have no direct meaning.",
  spearman: "Spearman correlation: a number from -1 to 1. Near 1 means two things rise together, near -1 means one rises as the other falls, near 0 means no clear link.",
  classifier: "Classifier: a model that learns from examples to sort things into groups, here guessing a model's origin, company or upload year from its benchmark scores.",
  test: "Test set: models held back during training, so the classifier is graded on models it has never seen.",
  baseline: "Baseline: the accuracy you would get by always guessing the most common group. A useful classifier should clearly beat it.",
  roc: "ROC curve: shows the trade-off between catching members of a group and wrongly flagging others, as the classifier is made more or less strict.",
  auc: "AUC (area under the curve): 0.5 means no better than a coin flip, 1.0 means perfect separation.",
  importance: "Feature importance: how much the classifier relied on each benchmark when making its guesses.",
};
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {
  document.querySelectorAll(".term").forEach(el => { el.tabIndex = 0; });
  tippy(".term", {
    content: el => GLOSSARY[el.dataset.term] || "",
    theme: "quarto",
    maxWidth: 320,
  });
});
</script>
```

```{ojs}
data = dataset === "hf" ? hf_data : eci_data
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
scoreHover = p => [
  p.Model,
  ...data.benchmarks.map(b => `${b}: ${p[b] != null ? p[b].toFixed(3) : "n/a"}`),
].join("<br>")
```

## PCA — 2D

*Which AI models have similar strengths and weaknesses?* Each dot is a model, placed by [PCA]{.term data-term="pca"}.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Each dot is one AI model. Hover over it to see its benchmark scores.
- Models with similar score patterns sit close together; models far apart performed differently.
- The axes are [principal components]{.term data-term="pc"}, not individual benchmarks. The percentage on each axis is its [explained variance]{.term data-term="variance"}.
- Colors show where the model's developer is based. If colors form separate clumps, models from different places tend to score differently.
- Scores are [standardized]{.term data-term="standardized"} first, and models without scores on every benchmark are left out.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = data.pca_2d;
  const colorField = data.color_fields[0];
  const groups = d3.group(d.points, p => (p[colorField] != null ? p[colorField] : "Unknown"));
  const traces = Array.from(groups, ([name, pts]) => ({
    x: pts.map(p => p.PC1),
    y: pts.map(p => p.PC2),
    text: pts.map(scoreHover),
    mode: "markers",
    type: "scatter",
    name: String(name),
    marker: {size: markerSize, opacity: 0.85},
    hovertemplate: "%{text}<extra>%{fullData.name}</extra>",
  }));

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    title: `PCA 2D — ${data.name}<br><sub>PC1 ${(d.variance[0]*100).toFixed(1)}% var · PC2 ${(d.variance[1]*100).toFixed(1)}% var</sub>`,
    xaxis: {title: `PC1 (${(d.variance[0]*100).toFixed(1)}%)`},
    yaxis: {title: `PC2 (${(d.variance[1]*100).toFixed(1)}%)`},
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.56),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```

## PCA — 3D

*The same picture as above, with a third axis for more detail.*

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Same as the 2D chart, plus a third [principal component]{.term data-term="pc"} (PC3) for depth.
- Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, and double-click to reset the view.
- Use it to check whether groups that overlap in 2D separate once you add depth.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = data.pca_3d;
  const colorField = data.color_fields[0];
  const groups = d3.group(d.points, p => (p[colorField] != null ? p[colorField] : "Unknown"));
  const traces = Array.from(groups, ([name, pts]) => ({
    x: pts.map(p => p.PC1),
    y: pts.map(p => p.PC2),
    z: pts.map(p => p.PC3),
    text: pts.map(scoreHover),
    mode: "markers",
    type: "scatter3d",
    name: String(name),
    marker: {size: markerSize3d, opacity: 0.85},
    hovertemplate: "%{text}<extra>%{fullData.name}</extra>",
  }));

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    title: `PCA 3D — ${data.name}`,
    scene: {
      xaxis: {title: `PC1 (${(d.variance[0]*100).toFixed(1)}%)`},
      yaxis: {title: `PC2 (${(d.variance[1]*100).toFixed(1)}%)`},
      zaxis: {title: `PC3 (${(d.variance[2]*100).toFixed(1)}%)`},
    },
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.56),
    paper_bgcolor: "white",
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```

## PCA — Loadings

*What do the PCA axes actually measure?* Each [loading]{.term data-term="loading"} shows how much a benchmark shapes each axis.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Each benchmark has one bar (or heatmap cell) per [principal component]{.term data-term="pc"}.
- Large values, positive or negative, mean that benchmark strongly drives that axis. Values near 0 mean it barely matters.
- The sign gives direction: on an axis with a positive loading, models further along that axis scored higher on that benchmark.
- If every benchmark has a similar loading on PC1, PC1 is roughly "overall ability".
- The heatmap shows the same numbers as the bar chart, with color for size and direction (see its color bar).
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = data.pca_loadings;
  const traces = d.components.map((comp, i) => ({
    x: d.benchmarks,
    y: d.matrix[i],
    name: comp,
    type: "bar",
  }));

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    barmode: "group",
    title: `PCA Loadings — ${data.name}`,
    xaxis: {tickangle: -30},
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.56),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
    shapes: [{type: "line", x0: 0, x1: 1, xref: "paper", y0: 0, y1: 0,
              line: {color: "black", width: 0.5}}],
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = data.pca_loadings;
  const traces = [{
    z: d.matrix,
    x: d.benchmarks,
    y: d.components,
    type: "heatmap",
    colorscale: "RdBu",
    zmid: 0,
    text: d.matrix.map(row => row.map(v => v.toFixed(3))),
    texttemplate: "%{text}",
    hovertemplate: "Benchmark: %{x}<br>Component: %{y}<br>Loading: %{z:.3f}<extra></extra>",
  }];

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    title: `PCA Loadings Heatmap — ${data.name}`,
    xaxis: {title: "Benchmark", tickangle: -30},
    yaxis: {title: "Principal Component"},
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.56),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```

## UMAP — 2D

*Another way to find clusters of similar models,* using [UMAP]{.term data-term="umap"}.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Like PCA, each dot is a model and similar models end up near each other.
- UMAP is better at revealing tight clusters, but **the axes have no units or meaning**, and the distance between two far-apart clusters doesn't tell you how different they are.
- Focus on which models clump together and whether a cluster is mostly one color.
- The next chart shows which benchmarks line up with each UMAP axis.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = data.umap_2d;
  const colorField = data.color_fields[0];
  const groups = d3.group(d.points, p => (p[colorField] != null ? p[colorField] : "Unknown"));
  const traces = Array.from(groups, ([name, pts]) => ({
    x: pts.map(p => p.UMAP1),
    y: pts.map(p => p.UMAP2),
    text: pts.map(scoreHover),
    mode: "markers",
    type: "scatter",
    name: String(name),
    marker: {size: markerSize, opacity: 0.85},
    hovertemplate: "%{text}<extra>%{fullData.name}</extra>",
  }));

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    title: `UMAP 2D — ${data.name}<br><sub>n_neighbors=${d.n_neighbors}, min_dist=${d.min_dist}</sub>`,
    xaxis: {title: "UMAP1"},
    yaxis: {title: "UMAP2"},
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.56),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```

## UMAP — Dimension Correlation

*Which benchmarks line up with the UMAP axes?* Measured with [Spearman correlation]{.term data-term="spearman"}.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Each bar compares one benchmark with one UMAP axis.
- Near +1: models further along that axis tend to score higher on that benchmark. Near −1: they tend to score lower. Near 0: no clear link.
- This gives the otherwise meaningless UMAP axes a rough interpretation.
- The heatmap shows the same numbers in color.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = data.umap_correlations;
  const traces = ["UMAP1", "UMAP2"].map(dim => ({
    x: d.benchmarks,
    y: d[dim],
    name: dim,
    type: "bar",
  }));

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    barmode: "group",
    title: `UMAP Dimension Correlation — Spearman r — ${data.name}`,
    yaxis: {range: [-1, 1], title: "Spearman r"},
    xaxis: {tickangle: -30},
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.56),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
    shapes: [{type: "line", x0: 0, x1: 1, xref: "paper", y0: 0, y1: 0,
              line: {color: "black", width: 0.5}}],
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```


## Custom-Axis Scatter

*Compare any two benchmarks directly.* Pick the axes and coloring below.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Each dot is a model. Its position shows its actual score on the two benchmarks you picked, with no transformation.
- Dots toward the top right did well on both; a rising diagonal pattern means the two benchmarks tend to agree.
- Change "Color By" to see whether origin, company or year groups score differently.
- Only models with scores on both benchmarks are shown; the count is under the title.
:::

::: {.controls-row}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof scatter_x = Inputs.select(data.benchmarks, {
  label: "X Axis",
  value: data.benchmarks[0],
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof scatter_y = Inputs.select(data.benchmarks, {
  label: "Y Axis",
  value: data.benchmarks.length > 1 ? data.benchmarks[1] : data.benchmarks[0],
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof scatter_color = Inputs.select(data.color_fields, {
  label: "Color By",
  value: data.color_fields[0],
})
```

:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const pts = data.scatter_data.points.filter(
    p => p[scatter_x] != null && p[scatter_y] != null
  );
  const groups = d3.group(pts, p => String(p[scatter_color] != null ? p[scatter_color] : "Unknown"));
  const traces = Array.from(groups, ([name, points]) => ({
    x: points.map(p => p[scatter_x]),
    y: points.map(p => p[scatter_y]),
    text: points.map(p => p.Model),
    mode: "markers",
    type: "scatter",
    name,
    marker: {size: markerSizeScatter, opacity: 0.8},
    hovertemplate:
      `%{text}<br>${scatter_x}: %{x:.3f}<br>${scatter_y}: %{y:.3f}<extra>%{fullData.name}</extra>`,
  }));

  const n = pts.length;
  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    title: `${scatter_y} vs ${scatter_x}<br><sub>${n} models</sub>`,
    xaxis: {title: scatter_x},
    yaxis: {title: scatter_y},
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.56),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```

## Classifier

*Can you tell where a model comes from just by its benchmark scores?* A [classifier]{.term data-term="classifier"} tries to guess.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Pick a classifier method, what it should guess (the target) and which models to include.
- The classifier learns from three quarters of the models, then is graded on the remaining quarter, the [test set]{.term data-term="test"}.
- Only the 8 most common groups are kept, and groups with fewer than 3 models are dropped.
- If it guesses well above the [baseline]{.term data-term="baseline"}, models from different groups really do have different benchmark "fingerprints".
:::

::: {.controls-row}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof clf_type = Inputs.select(["svm", "dt", "lr"], {
  label: "Classifier",
  format: x => ({"svm": "SVM (RBF)", "dt": "Decision Tree", "lr": "Logistic Regression"})[x],
  value: "svm"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
clf_target_keys = Object.keys(data.classifier_targets)
viewof clf_target = Inputs.select(clf_target_keys, {
  label: "Target",
  format: x => data.classifier_targets[x].label,
  value: clf_target_keys[0]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
clf_origin_keys = Object.keys(data.classifier_origin_filters)
viewof clf_origins = Inputs.select(clf_origin_keys, {
  label: "Origin Filter",
  format: x => data.classifier_origin_filters[x].label,
  value: clf_origin_keys[0]
})
```

:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
clf_key = `${clf_type}|${clf_target}|${clf_origins}`
clf_result = data.classifier_results.hasOwnProperty(clf_key) ? data.classifier_results[clf_key] : null
```

### Confusion Matrix

*Where does the classifier get it right, and what does it confuse?*

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Rows are the true group and columns are the classifier's guess.
- The diagonal from top left to bottom right shows correct guesses; anything off it is a mistake.
- Numbers are counts of models. Darker color means a higher share of that row, so each row's colors show how that group's models were labeled.
- Compare the accuracy in the title with the "always guessing" [baseline]{.term data-term="baseline"}. A small gap means the classifier learned little.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  if (!clf_result)
    return html`<p style="color:#888"><em>Not enough data for this combination.</em></p>`;

  const d = clf_result;
  const cm_norm = d.cm.map(row => {
    const s = row.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) || 1;
    return row.map(v => v / s);
  });

  const traces = [{
    z: cm_norm,
    x: d.labels,
    y: d.labels,
    type: "heatmap",
    colorscale: [[0, "#e0e0e0"], [0.5, "#6baed6"], [1, "#08519c"]],
    zmin: 0, zmax: 1,
    text: d.cm,
    texttemplate: "%{text}",
    hovertemplate: "True: %{y}<br>Pred: %{x}<br>Count: %{text}<br>Rate: %{z:.1%}<extra></extra>",
  }];

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    title: `Confusion Matrix — ${d.clf_name} predicting ${d.target_label}<br><sub>Accuracy: ${(d.accuracy*100).toFixed(1)}% (always guessing ${d.baseline_label}: ${(d.baseline_accuracy*100).toFixed(1)}%) · ${d.n_test} test samples · Origins: ${d.origin_label}</sub>`,
    xaxis: {title: "Predicted"},
    yaxis: {title: "True", autorange: "reversed"},
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.8),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```

### ROC Curve

*How well does the classifier separate each group from the rest?* Shown as an [ROC curve]{.term data-term="roc"}.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- There is one curve per group. Curves bowing toward the top left corner are better.
- The dashed diagonal is random guessing.
- Each curve's [AUC]{.term data-term="auc"} sums it up as one number: 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect. The title shows the average across groups.
- AUC for small groups is less reliable because few test models are behind it.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  if (!clf_result) return html``;

  const d = clf_result;
  const traces = Object.values(d.roc).map(r => ({
    x: r.fpr,
    y: r.tpr,
    mode: "lines",
    name: `${r.label} (AUC=${r.auc.toFixed(3)})`,
  }));

  traces.push({
    x: [0, 1], y: [0, 1],
    mode: "lines",
    line: {dash: "dash", color: "gray"},
    name: "Random (AUC=0.500)",
  });

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    title: `ROC Curve — ${d.clf_name} predicting ${d.target_label}<br><sub>Macro AUC: ${d.macro_auc.toFixed(3)}</sub>`,
    xaxis: {title: "False Positive Rate", constrain: "domain", scaleanchor: "y"},
    yaxis: {title: "True Positive Rate", constrain: "domain"},
    width: Math.min(width, 800), height: Math.min(width, 800),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
    legend: {x: 0.6, y: 0.05},
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```

### Feature Importances

*Which benchmarks did the classifier rely on most?* See [feature importance]{.term data-term="importance"}.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this chart
- Longer bars mean the classifier leaned more on that benchmark to tell groups apart.
- For Decision Tree, this is how much each benchmark improved its splits. For Logistic Regression, it is the average size of each benchmark's weight.
- SVM has no built-in measure, so nothing is shown for it.
- Importance shows what helps tell groups apart, not which benchmark is "better".
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  if (!clf_result || !clf_result.importances)
    return html`<p style="color:#888"><em>No feature importances for this classifier (SVM has none natively).</em></p>`;

  const d = clf_result;
  const entries = Object.entries(d.importances).sort((a, b) => a[1] - b[1]);

  const traces = [{
    y: entries.map(e => e[0]),
    x: entries.map(e => e[1]),
    type: "bar",
    orientation: "h",
  }];

  const div = document.createElement("div");
  Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, {
    title: `Feature Importances — ${d.clf_name}`,
    xaxis: {title: "Importance"},
    width: width, height: Math.round(width * 0.56),
    paper_bgcolor: "white", plot_bgcolor: "white",
  }, {responsive: true});
  return div;
}
```
